thesis: The skills ranking weighs entry difficulty, defensibility and earning potential under uncertain AI change.
summary: Nineteen skills span social management, speaking, trades, project management, sales, SEO/AEO, data analysis, media buying, design, security, prompting, email, editing, lead generation, trading, copywriting, development and automation. Martell favors speaking, sales and demand generation, treats media judgment as useful despite execution pressure, and explicitly assigns no S tier. He repeatedly revises placements and encourages choosing one skill rather than all.

review_status: Codex editorial draft; complete local transcript read; claims not independently verified
synthesis_method: Direct Codex extraction from complete local transcript; exact quotations verified locally
context_and_limits: A subjective ranking from his hiring/spending experience, not a labor-market study. Salary, displacement, model and technical claims are unverified forecasts or anecdotes. He distinguishes trade employment from owning a scalable trade business. Low entry barriers do not imply competence; generated code is not demonstrated production engineering. Some placements value strategic learning despite lower expected pay, so the criteria are not consistently weighted.
review_changes: Restores no-S-tier conclusion, live revisions, his specific interested-lead definition and differences between execution, taste and scalable ownership.
